title: Management Functions
description: The management functions exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), bars efficiency surveys and activities relating to management functions or techniques.
summary: The management functions exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) bars efficiency surveys and activities relating to management functions or techniques—such as financial data preparation, employee training programs, management organization plans, and management-based production changes—from the U.S. R&D tax credit. For wages, only first-line supervision counts as direct supervision, and wages below the 80% threshold are prorated, not forfeited.

body.text: The management functions exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) bars efficiency surveys and activities relating to management functions or techniques—such as financial data preparation, employee training programs, management organization plans, and management-based production changes—from the U.S. R&D tax credit. For wages, only first-line supervision counts as direct supervision, and wages below the 80% threshold are prorated, not forfeited.

Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, management functions occupy a dual legal boundary separating non-qualified business administration from creditable technical experimentation and research oversight. At the activity level, Congress excludes any efficiency survey and any activity relating to a management function or technique from the statutory definition of qualified research. At the wage-expenditure level, Treasury Regulations permit in-house labor costs for the immediate first-line supervision of qualified research, while categorically disqualifying higher-level executive oversight as well as administrative, financial, or personnel supervision.

Regulatory citations to 26 CFR §§ 1.41-2 and 1.41-4 reflect the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) text current as of October 30, 2026 (last amended October 26, 2026, with section metadata updated November 9, 2026), supplemented for 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5) by the 2015 Code of Federal Regulations edition matching the current section structure in 26 CFR § 1.41-0. Statutory citations reflect published and preliminary United States Code editions whose amendment notes extend through 2018 without any subsequent 2025 statutory amendments to the management functions exclusion.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework for Management Functions
Statutory Basis and Legislative Purpose

To qualify for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41, a taxpayer's research activities must satisfy the four-part statutory test codified in IRC § 41(d)(1), applied separately to each discrete business component pursuant to the shrinking-back and component rules of IRC § 41(d)(2)(A). Specifically, expenditures must be eligible under IRC § 174 (characterized in post-2017 statutory text and administrative rulings as specified research or experimental expenditures), undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3). Under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A), a qualified purpose exists only if the research relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Baseline summaries that omit "or quality" from the enumeration of qualified purposes truncate the statutory standard; IRS audit guidelines and statutory text explicitly encompass all four criteria.

Even where systematic study, evaluation, or analytical modeling occurs, the statutory exclusions enumerated in IRC § 41(d)(4) bar non-technical, administrative, or routine commercial activities from qualifying for the tax credit. Baseline compliance materials frequently misattribute the management functions exclusion to IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and characterize the exclusion as an administrative boundary originated by the IRS. Both propositions are legally inaccurate and require correction. First, Congress—rather than the IRS—enacted the statutory exclusions in the Tax Reform Act of 1986 after determining that taxpayers had previously construed the definition of qualified research overly broadly to claim tax credits for virtually any commercial product-development or operational expense. Second, IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) governs the statutory exclusion for any activity relating to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. The statutory exclusions for efficiency surveys and activities relating to management functions or techniques are codified specifically at IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(i) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(ii), respectively.

From a second-order structural perspective, the placement of the management functions exclusion within IRC § 41(d)(4) means that it operates as an absolute statutory bar rather than a mere evidentiary presumption. Even if an organizational restructuring study or workflow analysis utilizes sophisticated mathematical modeling or statistical software, Congress determined that improvements in managerial efficiency or administrative organization lie outside the technological experimentation domain that IRC § 41 was designed to subsidize.
Enumerated Management Exclusions and Production Process Boundaries

Implementing the congressional mandate of IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)—rather than 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), which is erroneously cited in baseline reference tables and actually governs internal-use software—defines the regulatory scope of excluded surveys, studies, and management activities for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(i) and (ii), qualified research categorically excludes any efficiency survey as well as any activity relating to a management function or technique. The regulation specifies that the phrase "management function or technique" includes the preparation of financial data and analysis, the development of employee training programs and management organization plans, and management-based changes in production processes. Both the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software and the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) reiterate this regulatory enumeration verbatim and supply the explicit parenthetical example of rearranging work stations on an assembly line. By contrast, granular sub-examples such as "cost accounting, budgetary forecasting, and complex financial modeling" represent analytical illustrations of financial data preparation rather than verbatim regulatory phrasing within 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(ii).

body.text: This regulatory taxonomy establishes a critical operational-versus-technical dichotomy in manufacturing, industrial engineering, and commercial production environments. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component that must independently satisfy the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1) without taking into account research relating to the manufactured product itself. Consequently, modifying an assembly line, manufacturing cell, or production workflow qualifies as creditable research only if the activities constitute a process of experimentation grounded in physical, biological, engineering, or computer sciences to resolve technological uncertainty—such as uncertainty regarding mechanical equipment capability, automated robotics integration, or material performance under thermal stress. Conversely, reorganizing work stations, re-sequencing operator tasks, or implementing lean manufacturing principles solely for throughput optimization, labor ergonomics, or logistical efficiency falls squarely within the management-based production process exclusion of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9.

Furthermore, IRS software audit guidelines extend the rationale of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9 to enterprise information technology acquisitions, noting that routine due diligence and product selection studies—such as evaluating competing database management systems, computer hardware manufacturers, enterprise resource planning (ERP) vendors, or web portal platforms—constitute excluded management decision-making rather than technological experimentation. This administrative interpretation creates a significant ripple effect for corporate IT claims: time spent by senior systems architects comparing vendor capabilities or benchmarking commercial off-the-shelf software packages must be segregated from subsequent engineering activities aimed at resolving true architectural or integration uncertainties.
Interlocking Exclusions and Financial Product Research

Within the statutory architecture of IRC § 41(d)(4)(D), the management functions exclusion operates alongside three adjacent exclusions codified in IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(iii)–(v) and implemented in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(iii)–(v): market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions); routine data collections; and routine or ordinary testing or inspections for quality control. In corporate practice, these provisions frequently overlap—management feasibility studies routinely incorporate market research, and industrial efficiency surveys rely heavily on routine data collections. Because each subsection of IRC § 41(d)(4) functions as an independent disqualifier, a taxpayer must clear every applicable exclusion before any portion of an activity can be treated as qualified research.

In evaluating financial product development, baseline compliance analyses frequently introduce a multi-part citation and legal classification error regarding 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10. First, baseline summary tables occasionally mis-cite this regulatory illustration as Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), Example 10, whereas its actual codification in the Code of Federal Regulations is 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10. Second, baseline descriptions often misstate one of the underlying factual inputs of the example as "demand volatility," whereas the final regulations in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 (69 FR 22, published January 2, 2004) state precisely that an insurance company researched the effect of pricing and tax consequences on demand for a new life insurance product, the expected volatility of interest rates, and expected mortality rates based on published data and prior insurance claims.

Third, and most substantively from a legal standpoint, baseline commentary erroneously asserts that 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10 classifies actuarial modeling, economic modeling, market analysis, and regulatory compliance for financial product viability as "either management functions or market research". Both T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22) and the IRS Software Audit Guidelines explicitly hold instead that the insurance company's activities in Example 10 constitute research in the social sciences (including economics and business management), which is barred under the separate statutory exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and its implementing regulation at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8)—not under the management functions or market research provisions of IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). While the practical compliance takeaway remains sound—namely, that financial services institutions must isolate qualifying software engineering and algorithmic computing architectures from product pricing, actuarial analysis, and economic feasibility modeling—attributing Example 10 to the management functions exclusion misidentifies the controlling statutory authority.
Management Functions in Internal Use Software and Organizational Contexts
General and Administrative Functions in Internal Use Software

In corporate software development claims, the management functions exclusion intersects directly with the statutory regime governing internal-use software (IUS) under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), which was promulgated as a final rule on October 4, 2016 (FR Doc 2016-23174) following the issuance of proposed regulations on January 20, 2015 (FR Doc 2015-00690). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A), software is presumed to be developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use if the software is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business.

Baseline technical reports often identify only two G&A categories: financial management and human resources management. However, the authoritative text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B) establishes three distinct G&A subdivisions. The first subdivision covers financial management functions under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1), which explicitly include supporting recordkeeping. The second subdivision encompasses human resources management functions under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(2), illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii), Example 3 by software developed to interact with existing payroll software so that employees can print pay stubs and modify tax deductions online. The third subdivision captures support services functions under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3), illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii), Example 4 by website software developed to facilitate marketing and advertising.

Omitting the third category (support services) creates a substantial blind spot in audit defense, because administrative support software—such as internal ticketing, facility management, or marketing support systems—is subject to the exact same IUS classification rules as financial and human resources applications. Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii), Example 5 confirms that middleware or data-migration software developed to transfer data from legacy financial, human resources, inventory, and sales systems into a new enterprise resource management system falls within 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B) as internal-use software. Conversely, software that is intended from the outset of development to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(A), or software developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(B), is not treated as developed primarily for internal use, while dual-function software (serving both G&A and third-party functions) is governed by the bifurcation and safe-harbor rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi).

Available primary excerpts of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) confirm that financial management functions include supporting recordkeeping and are introduced with the open-ended regulatory phrasing "Financial management functions include, but are not limited to," while the 2015 and 2016 Federal Register preambles confirm that G&A functions encompass financial management, human resources management, and support services.

More critically, baseline compliance instructions frequently contradict both themselves and the regulatory structure of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) regarding the procedural relationship between G&A functions and the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). As corroborated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii), Examples 17 and 18, internal-use software can qualify for the research credit only if it satisfies both the general four-part test of IRC § 41(d) (while not being otherwise excluded) and the three-prong HTI test. Under the first prong of the HTI test, the software must be innovative, meaning it would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful. Under the second prong, the software development must involve significant economic risk, meaning the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. Under the third prong, the software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer in that the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

Baseline compliance recommendations sometimes instruct taxpayers that all development costs for financial management or human resources functionalities "must be strictly segregated and excluded from QREs before the software proceeds to the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test". That directive inverts the regulatory sequence established in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6). Under the Treasury Regulations, determining that software performs a G&A function (financial management, human resources management, or support services) under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B) is the exact predicate that classifies the software as internal-use software and subjects it to the HTI test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). If G&A software costs were automatically excluded prior to the HTI test, the HTI test would have no statutory or regulatory function to perform. Rather, G&A software development expenditures are excluded from qualified research expenses (QREs) only if the software fails to satisfy the three-prong HTI test (or fails the threshold requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) or an independent exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)).
Human Resources, Training, and Organizational Planning

Outside the realm of internal-use software, human resources management, personnel administration, and organizational planning are categorically excluded from the research credit under both the activity-level rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5) and the wage-service rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c). At the activity level, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(ii) explicitly excludes the development of employee training programs and management organization plans from qualified research. At the expenditure level, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) stipulates that general administrative services not sufficiently closely related to research do not qualify as "direct support" of research. The regulation provides three concrete examples of excluded personnel: payroll personnel who prepare salary checks for laboratory scientists, accountants who account for research expenses, and "officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters". Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) emphasizes that these administrative, financial, and personnel services remain disqualified even when the individuals performing them are formally assigned to or housed within the research department rather than a separate corporate department.

Consequently, when engineering directors, laboratory heads, or technical project leads devote time to drafting departmental restructuring proposals, writing employee job descriptions, designing training or compliance curricula, conducting annual performance evaluations, or formulating salary and bonus plans, those hours must be excluded from eligible wage QREs. While those specific operational task descriptions represent practical compliance elaborations rather than verbatim regulatory text, their exclusion is directly mandated by the combined operation of 26 CFR §§ 1.41-2(c)(3) and 1.41-4(c)(5)(ii).
Direct Supervision, Wage Allocation, and Audit Risk
First-Line Direct Supervision Versus Higher-Level and General Management

In evaluating the eligibility of managerial compensation, practitioners frequently conflate the activity exclusions of IRC § 41(d) with the wage-service rules of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c). Baseline educational modules occasionally state that 26 CFR § 1.41-2 excludes management functions from qualified research activities (QRAs) while carving out an exception for "direct supervision," and further assert that "the eligibility of a manager's time does not depend on their job title (e.g., CTO or Engineering VP) but rather on the specific nature of their day-to-day involvement in the technical uncertainty resolution process". Both statements contain fundamental legal errors that expose taxpayers to severe IRS audit adjustments.

First, 26 CFR § 1.41-2 does not define qualified research activities (which are governed by IRC § 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4); instead, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c) defines "qualified services" for purposes of determining in-house research wage expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), an employee performs "qualified services" across three enumerated statutory and regulatory categories: engaging in qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1), which means the actual conduct of qualified research (as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments); engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2); or engaging in the direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3).

Second, asserting that a Chief Technology Officer (CTO) or Vice President of Engineering can claim "direct supervision" wages regardless of organizational hierarchy directly violates the plain text of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2). That regulation defines "direct supervision" strictly as "the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments)". The regulation then establishes an explicit bright-line prohibition: "'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) reinforces this boundary by stating: "Direct support does not include supervision. Supervisory services constitute 'qualified services' only to the extent provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section".

The second-order legal implication of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) is profound: organizational reporting structure directly controls the eligibility of supervisory time. In a multi-tiered engineering organization where software engineers or laboratory researchers report to first-line Engineering Managers or Team Leads, who in turn report to a Director of R&D, Vice President of Engineering, or CTO, none of the supervisory activities performed by the Director, Vice President, or CTO qualify as "direct supervision" under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)—even when that executive possesses an advanced scientific degree and reviews technical milestones or directs testing priorities through subordinate managers. Unless the organization is flat (such that researchers report directly to the Vice President or CTO without intermediate first-line managers), a higher-level executive's compensation can qualify under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c) only for the specific hours the executive personally spends conducting hands-on qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1) (such as personally writing experimental source code, authoring technical architecture specifications to resolve technological uncertainty, or personally executing prototype tests) or performing non-supervisory direct support under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3).

body.text: The Substantially All Rule and Proportional Wage Allocation

The most consequential computational error in baseline analyses of the management functions exclusion involves an inverted interpretation of the 80% "substantially all" rule for employee wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2). Baseline narrative text frequently presents a scenario in which an R&D Director dedicates 25% of annual working time to excluded management functions and asserts that, because of the 80% "substantially all" threshold, dedicating more than 20% of an employee's time to non-qualified activities causes 100% of that employee's annual wages to be disallowed as QREs. Elsewhere, baseline prose repeats this forfeiture theory by claiming that if an employee's qualified research time drops from 80% to 79% (with 21% spent on administrative management), the taxpayer is forced to disallow 100% of that employee's wages rather than just the 21% attributable to administrative duties.

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1), when an employee performs both qualified services and nonqualified services during a taxable year, the taxpayer does not forfeit the employee's wages; instead, only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense. Specifically, in the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the eligible wage QRE is calculated by multiplying the total amount of wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year by the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of qualified services to the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year. Expressed mathematically, for an employee with total annual IRC § 3401(a) wages Wtotal, time spent in qualified services Tqual, and total working time Ttotal, the qualified service ratio Rqual is:
Rqual = Tqual / Ttotal

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and (2), the resulting qualified wage expenditure WQRE is governed by a piecewise function where the 80% threshold operates exclusively as an upward safe harbor rather than a downward forfeiture cliff:
WQRE = Wtotal if Rqual ≥ 0.80
WQRE = Wtotal × Rqual if Rqual < 0.80

Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) provides that if the wages allocated under paragraph (d)(1) to services meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii)—which encompasses all three categories of qualified services (engaging in qualified research, direct supervision, and direct support), not solely "qualified research" as narrowly stated in baseline prose—constitute at least 80% of the total wages paid or incurred for the employee during the taxable year, then substantially all of the services performed by that employee are treated as qualified services, allowing 100% of the employee's wages to be claimed as QREs. Conversely, if the employee's qualified service ratio is below 80%, the taxpayer simply claims the proportional fraction Wtotal × Rqual under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and excludes the nonqualified fraction Wtotal × (1 − Rqual).

Practitioners must also distinguish the employee-level wage safe harbor in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) from the separate business-component-level "substantially all" requirement under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)—which retained the structure described in the 2001 proposed regulations (REG-112991-01) when finalized in T.D. 9104—the requirement that "substantially all" of the activities of a research project constitute elements of a process of experimentation is satisfied only if 80% or more of the research activities (measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, and determined without regard to the employee wage safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)) constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Conflating the activity-level experimentation threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) with the employee-level wage allocation rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) is the root cause of the erroneous forfeiture-cliff claim.

In Hypothetical Example 1 (evaluating an R&D Director with 25% excluded management time), assume an R&D Director earning Wtotal = $200,000 in annual W-2 wages spends 75% of total annual working hours (Rqual = 0.75) personally engaging in hands-on qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1) and 25% of annual working hours (1 − Rqual = 0.25) on excluded management functions under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5), applying the default time-ratio allocation of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1). Because Rqual = 0.75 < 0.80, the 100% safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) is not triggered. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1), however, the taxpayer claims the proportional qualified wage allocation:

The taxpayer excludes only the administrative portion ($200,000 × 0.25 = $50,000), rather than forfeiting the entire $200,000 salary. Notice the critical interaction with 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2): if that R&D Director's 75% technical involvement had instead consisted entirely of higher-level supervision over subordinate first-line engineering managers (rather than hands-on research under § 1.41-2(c)(1) or direct first-line supervision of researchers under § 1.41-2(c)(2)), then 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) would disqualify the entire 75% supervisory component, reducing WQRE to $0 regardless of whether general administrative duties accounted for 25% or 5% of the Director's year.

In Hypothetical Example 2 (evaluating a first-line Engineering Manager across 30%, 79%, and 80% qualified service ratios), assume a first-line manager earning Wtotal = $200,000 performs qualifying first-line direct supervision and hands-on research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(2). At a 30% qualified service share (70% excluded general management), proportional allocation yields WQRE = $200,000 × 0.30 = $60,000 (with $140,000 excluded). At a 79% qualified service share (21% excluded general management), proportional allocation yields WQRE = $200,000 × 0.79 = $158,000 (with $42,000 excluded). When qualified services reach 80% (leaving 20% excluded general management), the safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) brings 100% of the employee's wages into QREs, yielding WQRE = $200,000 × 1.00 = $200,000 ($0 excluded). Thus, the marginal impact of dropping from 80% to 79% qualified services is the loss of the 21% administrative safe-harbor bonus ($42,000), not a $200,000 total disallowance.

body.text: From an audit defense standpoint, a 100% disallowance of an employee's wages below the 80% threshold occurs only when a taxpayer fails its burden of proof under IRC § 6001 by failing to maintain sufficient credible records to substantiate a reasonable basis for estimating the employee's proportional time allocation.
IRS Examination Focus on Management Time

When auditing Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), IRS examiners routinely scrutinize claims that include high-salaried executives, department heads, and project managers. The IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (both in its current online Qualified Research Expenses guidance and its republished 2008 reference edition) instructs examining agents verbatim: "Payroll records, employee job descriptions, performance evaluations, calendars and appointment books are good sources of information".

During an examination, agents cross-reference oral testimony or post-hoc allocation surveys against these contemporaneous non-tax business records. If an employee's formal corporate job description, annual performance evaluation, and Microsoft Outlook or Google Calendar entries demonstrate recurring involvement in annual budget planning, vendor contract negotiations, staffing interviews, PTO approvals, corporate strategy committees, or supervision of subordinate managers, the IRS will challenge inflated 80% "substantially all" claims and either reduce the qualified wage allocation proportionally under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) or disallow unsubstantiated supervisory time under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3).
Substantiation Standards, Operational Proposals, and Regulatory History
Legal Recordkeeping Rules Versus Unverified Compliance Proposals

A sound tax compliance strategy requires separating binding statutory and regulatory recordkeeping mandates from commercial best-practice frameworks marketed by software vendors and R&D tax consultancies. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d)—as established in T.D. 8930 (66 FR 289, January 3, 2001), modified and finalized in T.D. 9104 (69 FR 22, January 2, 2004), and applied in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide and state administrative rulings—a taxpayer claiming the research credit must satisfy the general federal recordkeeping requirements of IRC § 6001 and 26 CFR § 1.6001-1 by retaining records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit.

Tracing the regulatory history of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) illuminates why flexible substantiation rules prevail today. When Treasury and the IRS issued proposed regulations in 1998 (REG-105170-97, FR Doc 98-31528, December 2, 1998), they proposed a rigid documentation requirement mandating that taxpayers record the specific results of their four-step process of experimentation contemporaneously. Following extensive public comments objecting that mandatory research-specific documentation templates did not align with how commercial engineering teams operate, T.D. 8930 refocused the rule on IRC § 6001, and the preamble to the 2004 final regulations in T.D. 9104 explicitly confirmed that the final qualified research regulations "do not impose any recordkeeping requirement on taxpayers beyond the requirements set out in section 6001 and the regulations thereunder". At the wage level, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) defaults allocation to the ratio of "total time actually spent" in qualified services to total time spent in all services, unless the taxpayer demonstrates a more appropriate allocation method. At the project level, IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) requires that qualification be established separately for each business component.

By contrast, several highly prescriptive operational protocols presented in baseline compliance manuals derive from secondary literature or commercial software vendors rather than primary tax law. Specifically, these unverified secondary protocols include the three-tier time-tracking software taxonomy dividing records into "Client spaces," "Projects" (categorized into applied research or experimental development), and "Tasks" featuring a mandatory "Excluded Management Activities" label (attributed in baseline text to the commercial vendor My Hours), as well as the assertion that "Best practices require that activities and results be tracked as they occur, not retroactively" while linking labor granularly to cost centers, outside contractors, and material accounts (attributed in baseline text to the consultancy alliantgroup). Similarly unverified in primary authorities are the specific warning regarding the commingling of technical and administrative time in agile software workflows involving "sprint planning, stand-up meeting administration, or organizational charting" (attributed in baseline text to an October 2025 article in The Tax Adviser), the operational instruction to segregate labor, supplies, and contract research expenses for G&A software modules using specific supply-tracking commentary (attributed in baseline text to KBKG, though analytically consistent with the statutory rule that supplies and contract research are creditable under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (b)(3) only when used or performed in the conduct of qualified research), and the prescriptive compliance templates recommending structured "Functional Interviews," granular log entries contrasting "4 hours - Reviewing API Architecture" against "4 hours - Management," and a formal "Nexus" document illustrated with a hypothetical "Project Alpha".

While none of those proprietary software configurations, task tags, or template names are mandated by the Internal Revenue Code or Treasury Regulations, their underlying analytical objective aligns with sound audit risk management. Because IRS examiners inspect calendars, job descriptions, and performance reviews under the IRS ATG, voluntarily maintaining contemporaneous project-level time logs that separate administrative management (such as sprint scheduling, budgeting, and personnel reviews) from hands-on technical experimentation or immediate first-line supervision linked to identifiable IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) business components substantially strengthens a taxpayer's evidentiary posture under IRC § 6001.
Clarifying the 2004 Final Regulations and Withdrawn IUS ANPRM

Baseline compliance recommendations occasionally advise taxpayers and their legal counsel to consult "the 2004 Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) relating to the definition of qualified research," asserting that the IRS Audit Guidelines reference this 2004 ANPRM and that it details "how the IRS intended to differentiate between technical uncertainty and administrative uncertainty, particularly regarding new production processes or complex software that blends technical and organizational improvements".

A review of the Federal Register and IRS guidance confirms that this recommendation conflates two separate regulatory documents published on the same day—January 2, 2004. First, Treasury Decision 9104 (69 FR 22, FR Doc 03-31818, effective January 2, 2004, and also reproduced in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2004-06 IRB) promulgated the final regulations defining qualified research and the process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4 (including 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5) on management functions and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 1 through 10, while removing and reserving § 1.41-4(c)(6) for internal-use software). It is this final regulation—T.D. 9104—that the IRS Software Audit Guidelines quote and cite extensively when analyzing technical uncertainty, production processes, and the management functions exclusion, not an ANPRM.

Second, on that same date, Treasury and the IRS published a separate Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (REG-153656-03, 69 FR 43, FR Doc 03-31819, January 2, 2004) that addressed solely internal-use software under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and invited public comments on the definition of internal-use software. That 2004 ANPRM did not govern general qualified research definitions, management-based production process exclusions, or "administrative uncertainty". Furthermore, the 2004 ANPRM was formally withdrawn by Treasury and the IRS on January 20, 2015 (FR Doc 2015-00690) when the agency issued new proposed internal-use software regulations, which were subsequently finalized on October 4, 2016 (FR Doc 2016-23174) and codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6).

Accordingly, tax counsel evaluating complex boundaries between management functions, production processes, and internal-use software should rely on the binding final regulations in T.D. 8930, T.D. 9104, and the 2016 final IUS regulations codified in 26 CFR §§ 1.41-2 and 1.41-4, alongside current IRS audit guidelines, rather than a withdrawn 2004 ANPRM.

body.text: Conclusion and Audit-Readiness Synthesis

Navigating the management functions boundary under IRC § 41 requires coordinating two distinct legal analyses: screening activities at the business-component level under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)–(6), and scrutinizing employee reporting hierarchies and time allocations at the wage-expenditure level under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d). Taxpayers that rely on imprecise secondary summaries risk either over-claiming senior executive supervision in violation of the first-line management restriction of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) or prematurely abandoning valid proportional wage claims below the 80% threshold due to a misunderstanding of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2). Similarly, software claimants must apply the three-category G&A framework of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B) as the gateway to the three-prong HTI evaluation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii), while grounding all documentary substantiation in contemporaneous business records—job descriptions, calendars, performance reviews, and time allocations—that satisfy IRC § 6001 and withstand IRS Audit Techniques Guide scrutiny.
